One-Sided Randomization in Two-Sided Platform Experiments: Which Side Should be Randomized?

Ramesh Johari    Anushka Murthy
November 12, 2026
Abstract

Two-sided marketplace platforms often use randomized experiments to evaluate new features, raising the question of whether to randomize customers or listings. Randomizing the smaller (short) side can reduce interference bias due to weaker competition, while randomizing the larger (long) side provides a larger nominal sample, potentially reducing variance. On the surface, these competing considerations suggest a bias-variance trade-off in choosing which side to randomize. We investigate this trade-off in a two-sided marketplace with first-come, first-served (FCFS) booking and heterogeneous customer preferences, studying the bias and variance of difference-in-means estimators of the global average treatment effect.

Our findings suggest that rather than a bias-variance tradeoff, in fact short-side randomization is generally preferable on both dimensions. We prove these results in an asymptotic regime where market imbalance increases. We establish conditions under which (1) short-side randomization eliminates first-order interference bias, while long-side randomization retains it; and (2) short-side randomization also achieves a variance rate of no larger asymptotic order than long-side randomization. The key insight is that although the long side contains more participants, the number of matches is constrained by the population on the short side, limiting the apparent variance advantage of randomizing a larger sample. Our conditions accommodate heterogeneous preferences and treatment effects and are satisfied by familiar logit models of customer choice. Together, these findings support randomizing on the short side, despite the larger sample size available on the long side.

1 Introduction

Two-sided marketplace platforms routinely use randomized experiments (A/B tests) to evaluate new interventions and features: e.g., a new design for product listings, or a new search algorithm. The goal of such an experiment is typically to estimate the GATE (global average treatment effect) with respect to the number of matches. This is the difference in the number of matches between two counterfactual universes: one where the entire market is in the treatment condition (global treatment), and another where the entire market is in the control condition (global control). A common procedure to estimate the GATE is to randomize one side of the market (i.e. customers or listings) to treatment or control using simple i.i.d. Bernoulli randomization; collect the match outcomes after the experiment; and form a difference-in-means (DM) estimator for the GATE.

Because these platforms are two-sided, they face a choice: should they randomize on the demand side of the market (“customers”), or on the supply side of the market (“listings”)? We begin by noting that regardless of which side of the market is chosen, typical approaches to estimation (such as the use of the DM estimator) exhibit a well-known interference bias [5, 19], since both treated and control participants on one side interact with the same set of participants on the opposite side.

Two competing considerations inform the choice of which side to randomize; both depend centrally on which side of the market is more constrained. To fix terminology, we refer to the side of the market with fewer participants as the short side of the market, and the opposing side as the long side. One approach to making this choice relies on the intuition that the sample size is larger on the long side, and thus (naively) variance is lower by randomizing on the long side; this is a common view in practice, and leads to long-side randomization. On the other hand, prior work [19] establishes in a Markovian queueing model of a two-sided marketplace that the bias is lower when randomizing on the short-side. These effects seem in tension with each other, leaving practical guidance unclear.

To study this apparent bias–variance trade-off, we consider a model of randomized experiments in a two-sided marketplace with one-sided customer preferences and first-come, first-served (FCFS) allocation of listings. Customers arrive sequentially and may book one listing from available inventory according to potentially heterogeneous preferences, with each listing accommodating at most one customer. Our model captures marketplace settings in which customers select from available inventory and listings become unavailable once booked, as in many lodging and e-commerce platforms. We allow treatment to affect customer choice and consider two experiment designs: randomizing customers to treatment and control; or randomizing listings to treatment and control. For each design, we study the interference bias and variance of the difference-in-means estimator of the GATE. Our framework accommodates a broader class of customer choice models beyond the logit choice model studied in [19].

We focus on large, imbalanced marketplaces, studying sequences of markets in which both sides grow but the ratio of short-side to long-side participants approaches zero. Let sns_{n} denote the fraction of market participants on the short side, and let nn denote the total market size. Because the number of matches is bounded by the short-side population, the GATE is always at most of order sns_{n}. We therefore investigate whether interference bias remains at first order, Θ⁡(sn)\Theta(s_{n}), or whether the first-order bias vanishes, o⁡(sn)o(s_{n}). We also compare the asymptotic variance rates of the two experiment designs, studying conditions under which both achieve variance of order O⁡(sn/n)O(s_{n}/n) despite the long-side having a larger sample.

Our first set of results establishes two sufficient conditions under which short-side randomization eliminates first-order interference bias — i.e., the bias is o⁡(sn)o(s_{n}). The first condition, which we call near saturation, is that nearly all short-side participants are matched under both global treatment and control, as well as in the experiment. This condition arises naturally when listings are the short side, since in our model, listings do not hold preferences or reject bookings. The second condition applies when customers are the short side and does not require near saturation. Instead, we assume that customers’ preferred listings are not overly concentrated on a small subset of available listing inventory. Under this condition, the effect of competition on match outcomes is second-order, yielding a bias of O⁡(sn2)O(s_{n}^{2}) up to an exponentially small remainder.

In contrast, we show that long-side randomization can retain first-order interference bias, Θ⁡(sn)\Theta(s_{n}). We show that this bias arises because treatment can redistribute matches between treated and control participants even when its effect on the total number of matches is small. We then show that the consideration-set logit choice model of [19] satisfies the conditions of our short-side and long-side bias results, thereby extending their conclusions to a broader class of customer choice models.

We next turn to the variance of the two experiment designs. Although randomizing on the long side provides a larger nominal sample size, the number of matches is limited by the short-side population. Consequently, participants on the long side become increasingly unlikely to match as the market becomes more imbalanced, potentially offsetting the variance reduction associated with a larger sample. We formalize this intuition and show that the variance of the difference-in-means estimator is O⁡(sn/n)O(s_{n}/n) under both short-side and long-side randomization.

The remaining question is then whether long-side randomization can still produce a smaller variance of order o⁡(sn/n)o(s_{n}/n). In this direction, we establish sufficient conditions under which long-side randomization has variance Θ⁡(sn/n)\Theta(s_{n}/n), implying that short-side randomization has no larger-order asymptotic variance. When customers are scarce, we strengthen the bounded-concentration condition used in our bias analysis to hold throughout the booking process, and additionally require that both experiment groups attract nonvanishing demand. When listings are scarce, we instead require that treatment does not change the probability of booking any particular listing by more than a constant multiplicative factor, and that a nonvanishing fraction of listings are booked in expectation. These conditions ensure that there is sufficient uncertainty in how matches are distributed between the treatment and control groups. We again verify that these conditions hold in the consideration-set logit model of [19].

Our model and results thus demonstrate there is no tradeoff between bias and variance: short-side randomization has a lower-order asymptotic interference bias than long-side randomization, and an asymptotic variance rate of at most the same order. As noted above, our model is well-matched to many online platform settings with depletable inventory. Further the relevant conditions we use to establish our main results are relatively mild, and likely to be satisfied in most real-world platforms: they rule out highly concentrated customer preferences, and nearly deterministic allocation of matches between the treatment and control groups. These conditions accommodate heterogeneous preferences and treatment effects and are satisfied by familiar logit models of customer choice. For practitioners, our findings suggest that from a statistical standpoint, they should prefer randomizing on the short-side of the market.

Organization of the paper.

In Section 2 we introduce our model of experimentation in a two-sided market with one-sided preferences and first-come, first-served search. In Section 3 we present our bias results. In Section 4 we present our variance results. The proofs of the bias and variance results appear in Appendices A and B respectively.

1.1 Related Literature

Our paper contributes to the literature on experiment design in two-sided marketplaces, where competition for scarce matching opportunities creates interference between treatment and control participants. Prior work has studied the resulting estimation bias and developed approaches to mitigating interference in marketplace experiments [5, 4, 14, 16, 26]. Related work studies the estimation of treatment effects in market equilibrium [38, 28, 29].

The papers most closely related to ours study interference bias and variance in conventional one-sided marketplace experiments. In [19], the authors analyze customer- and listing-randomized experiments in a Markovian marketplace model and shows that randomizing the short side can reduce interference bias. Similarly, [22] studies the bias and variance of these designs in a stylized matching model and provides guidance on the choice of randomized side. We complement this work by analyzing sequential first-come, first-served matching with general, potentially heterogeneous customer preferences. Rather than imposing a particular parametric choice model or examining mean-field limits, we develop finite-market conditions under which randomizing the short side eliminates first-order interference bias, and conditions under which the variance rate of short-side randomization is no worse than that of long-side randomization. Our results thus address both components of the apparent bias–variance tradeoff in a sequential marketplace with indivisible inventory. Related work on marketplace estimators includes approaches based on shadow prices and optimization [8], inference under two-sided market randomization [25], and regression adjustment for double-randomization designs [35].

A complementary literature develops alternative experiment designs and estimators to mitigate interference. Two-sided and multiple-randomization designs exploit variation on both sides of a marketplace [19, 3, 27], and [9] proposes a double-diagonal estimator that uses cross-arm interactions to reduce bias under two-sided randomization. In another direction, [39] develops a randomization design for comparing predetermined matching plans using their alternating-path and cycle structure. Other approaches include clustered and network-based designs [37, 32, 31, 40], and marketplace-specific ranking designs [15]. Other work [33] studies the cost of separating treatment and control into isolated submarkets, which can reduce interference at the expense of thinning matching opportunities. Work on pricing experiments further develops alternative estimators and designs under marketplace congestion [12, 10]. In contrast to these approaches, we retain one-sided Bernoulli randomization and the standard difference-in-means estimator, and ask which side of the marketplace should be randomized.

Our analysis also relates to experimentation in dynamic systems, where treatment assignments can affect future system states and outcomes. Prior work studies estimation under Markovian models of interference [13, 23, 21], as well as experiment design and inference under temporal interference using switchback experiments [7, 6, 30]. Related work considers optimal treatment targeting in dynamic systems [17]. A complementary literature studies the implications of interference for experiment decision-making. In particular, [20] examines these impacts on hypothesis testing and launch decisions in inventory-constrained marketplaces, while [24] studies the selection of recommendation algorithms when shared learning generates interference. Our focus, in contrast, is on the bias and variance of the difference-in-means estimator arising from the choice of which side of a two-sided marketplace to randomize.

Finally, our work relates to the broader causal-inference literature on interference, including foundational frameworks for treatment effects under interference [18, 1], network randomization inference [2], and bipartite exposure mappings [41]. Recent work considers robust estimation when interference is only weakly restricted [11], and estimation or validation using network structure or temporal outcome information [34, 36]. Our work similarly exploits matching structure to obtain an understanding of the bias and variance of one-sided randomization.

2 Model and Experiment Design

We consider a two-sided marketplace in which customers arrive sequentially and choose among available listings. A customer can book at most one listing, and each listing can accommodate at most one customer. We use this model to compare two common ways of running an A/B experiment: randomizing customers or randomizing listings.

In this section, we introduce the market, the booking process, the estimand, the two experiment designs, and the estimator.

2.1 Market and customer preferences

Customers and listings.

There are two finite sets of participants: a set of customers 𝒞n\mathcal{C}_{n} with size NCN_{C}, and a set of listings 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n} with size NPN_{P}. Let n=NC+NPn=N_{C}+N_{P} denote the total market size. We assume preferences are one-sided, customers hold preferences over listings but each listing would accept any request to book it. Each customer can complete at most one booking, and each listing has unit capacity.

We study matching over a fixed time period, which we refer to as a matching cycle, following Bright et al. [8]. Unlike their centralized matching model, customers in our setting book listings sequentially as they arrive. Bookings are final within the matching cycle, so booked listings do not become available again, and customers who leave without booking do not return.

Customer preferences.

For each pair consisting of a customer i∈𝒞ni\in\mathcal{C}_{n} and a listing j∈𝒫nj\in\mathcal{P}_{n}, we assume each pair is given a treatment assignment wi​j∈{0,1}w_{ij}\in\{0,1\}, where wi​j=1w_{ij}=1 denotes treatment and wi​j=0w_{ij}=0 denotes control. Customer ii’s utility for booking listing jj is then given by

ui​j​(wi​j).u_{ij}(w_{ij}).

Note that this utility depends on the pair’s treatment assignment. We normalize the utility of not booking to zero. Thus, customer ii regards listing jj as acceptable under treatment wi​jw_{ij} if ui​j​(wi​j)>0u_{ij}(w_{ij})>0. Among acceptable listings, the customer prefers the listing with the highest utility. If multiple listings have the same utility, ties are broken according to a fixed rule.

The intervention may change which listings customers find acceptable, how customers rank acceptable listings, or both. We allow heterogeneous preferences across customers and listings without imposing a particular choice model. In particular, our framework accommodates the consideration-set logit model of Johari et al. [19], but does not require logit choice.

Random market primitives.

We allow utilities to depend on random customer and listing characteristics. For each customer ii, let ξi\xi_{i} denote a customer-specific random primitive; for each listing jj, let ζj\zeta_{j} denote a listing-specific random primitive. We assume that the collection

(ξi:i∈𝒞n),(ζj:j∈𝒫n)\bigl(\xi_{i}:i\in\mathcal{C}_{n}\bigr),\qquad\bigl(\zeta_{j}:j\in\mathcal{P}_{n}\bigr)

consists of mutually independent blocks, and that

ui​j​(w)=gi​j,w​(ξi,ζj),w∈{0,1}.u_{ij}(w)=g_{ij,w}(\xi_{i},\zeta_{j}),\qquad w\in\{0,1\}. (1)

Customers and listings can have heterogeneous characteristics. A customer’s random primitives may affect their preferences for multiple listings, while a listing’s random primitives may affect how multiple customers value that listing. Thus, preferences may be correlated across listings for a given customer and across customers for a given listing. These individual-level random primitives are independent of treatment assignment.

2.2 Customer-side sequential booking

FCFS booking and available listings.

Customers arrive in an exogenous order, indexed 1,…,NC1,\ldots,N_{C} for convenience. When customer ii arrives, the customer observes the listings that remain available and chooses the highest-ranked acceptable listing among them. If none are acceptable, the customer leaves without booking.

More formally, let 𝐰=(wi​j)\mathbf{w}=(w_{ij}) specify the treatment exposure for every customer–listing pair, and let 𝒜i​(𝐰)\mathcal{A}_{i}(\mathbf{w}) denote the listings available immediately before customer ii arrives. Initially, 𝒜1​(𝐰)=𝒫n\mathcal{A}_{1}(\mathbf{w})=\mathcal{P}_{n}. If the available set is nonempty and

maxj∈𝒜i​(𝐰)⁡ui​j​(wi​j)>0,\max_{j\in\mathcal{A}_{i}(\mathbf{w})}u_{ij}(w_{ij})>0,

customer ii books a listing attaining this maximum, using the fixed tie-breaking rule. That listing is removed from the available set before the next customer arrives. Otherwise, the available set is unchanged. The same procedure is applied to every customer in arrival order.

We refer to this allocation rule as first-come, first-served (FCFS) booking. It allows customers to substitute to lower-ranked listings when their preferred listings have already been booked. The relative ranking of the remaining listings is unchanged when an unavailable listing is removed.

Match outcomes.

Let Mn​(𝐰)M_{n}(\mathbf{w}) denote the matching that results from the FCFS booking process under treatment exposure vector 𝐰\mathbf{w}, given the realized customer and listing primitives. For every participant v∈𝒞n∪𝒫nv\in\mathcal{C}_{n}\cup\mathcal{P}_{n}, define

Yv​(𝐰)=𝟏​{v​ is matched in ​Mn​(𝐰)}.Y_{v}(\mathbf{w})=\mathbf{1}\{v\text{ is matched in }M_{n}(\mathbf{w})\}.

The total number of matches is

Kn​(𝐰)=∑i∈𝒞nYi​(𝐰)=∑j∈𝒫nYj​(𝐰).K_{n}(\mathbf{w})=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}_{n}}Y_{i}(\mathbf{w})=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{P}_{n}}Y_{j}(\mathbf{w}). (2)

Each booking is counted once on each side of the market. Our outcome of interest is the number of matches, rather than the identity or value of the selected customer–listing pairs.

The unit-capacity constraint creates interference between participants. For example, treating one customer may change the listing they book, which can change the options available to later customers. Similarly, changing the treatment status of one listing may alter which customer books it and the subsequent allocation of other listings.

2.3 Estimand: Global average treatment effect

Our estimand is the difference in expected matches between the global treatment market, where 𝐰=𝟏\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{1}, and global control market, where 𝐰=𝟎\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{0}. We normalize this difference by the total number of participants and refer to the resulting object as the global average treatment effect (GATE):

τn=1n​(𝔼⁡[Kn​(𝟏)]−𝔼⁡[Kn​(𝟎)]).\tau_{n}=\frac{1}{n}\left(\mathbb{E}[K_{n}(\mathbf{1})]-\mathbb{E}[K_{n}(\mathbf{0})]\right). (3)

Expectations in (3) are taken over the random market primitives.

2.4 Experiment designs

Binary treatment.

For each customer–listing pair (i,j)(i,j), treatment exposure wi​j∈{0,1}w_{ij}\in\{0,1\} determines whether the customer evaluates the listing under control, with utility ui​j​(0)u_{ij}(0), or treatment, with utility ui​j​(1)u_{ij}(1). We compare two experimental designs that randomize participants on either the customer side or the listing side.

Let πC\pi_{C} and πP\pi_{P} denote the treatment assignment probabilities under customer and listing randomization, respectively. We assume that for some ε>0\varepsilon>0,

ε≤πd≤1−ε,d∈{C,P}.\varepsilon\leq\pi_{d}\leq 1-\varepsilon,\qquad d\in\{C,P\}. (4)

Treatment assignments are independent across participants and independent of the market primitives.

Customer randomization.

Under a customer-randomized experiment, each customer i∈𝒞ni\in\mathcal{C}_{n} receives an assignment

WiC∼Bernoulli⁡(πC),W_{i}^{C}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_{C}),

independently across customers. Every interaction involving customer ii has treatment exposure given by that customer’s assignment:

wi​jC=WiC,i∈𝒞n,j∈𝒫n.w_{ij}^{C}=W_{i}^{C},\qquad i\in\mathcal{C}_{n},\ j\in\mathcal{P}_{n}. (5)

Thus, a treated customer evaluates all listings under treatment, while a control customer evaluates all listings under control. Treated and control customers compete for the same pool of available listings.

Listing randomization.

Under a listing-randomized experiment, each listing j∈𝒫nj\in\mathcal{P}_{n} receives an assignment

WjP∼Bernoulli⁡(πP),W_{j}^{P}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_{P}),

independently across listings. In this case, treatment exposure is determined by the listing’s assignment:

wi​jP=WjP,i∈𝒞n,j∈𝒫n.w_{ij}^{P}=W_{j}^{P},\qquad i\in\mathcal{C}_{n},\ j\in\mathcal{P}_{n}. (6)

An arriving customer may therefore encounter both treated and control listings and compare them.

Let MndM_{n}^{d} denote the matching obtained under the experiment that randomizes side dd, and let YvdY_{v}^{d} be participant vv’s booking outcome under the matching. The two experimental designs generally produce different matchings, even though they evaluate the same underlying intervention. Under customer randomization, capacity constraints create interference because bookings change the listings available to subsequent customers. Under listing randomization, interference also arises because customers choose between treated and control listings, so treatment can shift bookings between the two groups.

2.5 Estimator and market imbalance

Difference-in-means estimator.

For a side-dd experiment, where d∈{C,P}d\in\{C,P\}, let 𝒟d\mathcal{D}_{d} denote the set of participants on the randomized side and NdN_{d} its size. For w∈{0,1}w\in\{0,1\}, define

Nd,w\displaystyle N_{d,w} =∑v∈𝒟d𝟏{Wvd=w},\displaystyle=\sum_{v\in\mathcal{D}_{d}}\mathbf{1}\{W_{v}^{d}=w\}, (7)
Kd,w\displaystyle K_{d,w} =∑v∈𝒟d𝟏{Wvd=w}Yvd.\displaystyle=\sum_{v\in\mathcal{D}_{d}}\mathbf{1}\{W_{v}^{d}=w\}Y_{v}^{d}.

Thus, Nd,wN_{d,w} is the number of participants assigned to treatment ww, while Kd,wK_{d,w} is the number of those participants who match. We study the usual difference-in-means estimator, rescaled by the randomized side’s share of the market:

Δ^d,n=Ndn​(Kd,1Nd,1−Kd,0Nd,0).\widehat{\Delta}_{d,n}=\frac{N_{d}}{n}\left(\frac{K_{d,1}}{N_{d,1}}-\frac{K_{d,0}}{N_{d,0}}\right). (8)

Because participants on one side compete for the same constrained set of participants on the other side, the outcome of a treated participant may depend on the assignments of other participants. Consequently, (8) need not be unbiased for (3). We compare the two experiments using the bias and variance

Bd,n=𝔼⁡[Δ^d,n]−τn,Vd,n=Var⁡(Δ^d,n).B_{d,n}=\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\Delta}_{d,n}]-\tau_{n},\qquad V_{d,n}=\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\Delta}_{d,n}). (9)

Throughout the rest of this paper, these expectations and variances include randomness from treatment assignment and random market primitives.

Market imbalance.

We study how the bias and variance of the two experiment designs change as the market becomes imbalanced in either direction. Let

mn=min⁡{NC,NP},ℓn=max⁡{NC,NP},sn=mnn.m_{n}=\min\{N_{C},N_{P}\},\qquad\ell_{n}=\max\{N_{C},N_{P}\},\qquad s_{n}=\frac{m_{n}}{n}. (10)

There are two distinct cases: customers may be scarce, with NC=mnN_{C}=m_{n}, or listings may be scarce, with NP=mnN_{P}=m_{n}. We also refer to these markets as demand-constrained or suppy-constrained respectively. Since each match uses one participant from each side, Kn​(𝐰)≤mnK_{n}(\mathbf{w})\leq m_{n}, and thus |τn|≤sn|\tau_{n}|\leq s_{n}.

We study the bias and variance of these estimators along these sequences of increasingly large and imbalanced markets. With sn=mn/ns_{n}=m_{n}/n denoting the short side’s share of the market, we study the bias relative to sns_{n} and the variance relative to sn/ns_{n}/n.

3 Bias

In this section, we study how the bias of the difference-in-means estimator behaves under each experiment design when one side of the market is much smaller than the other.

We establish two different sufficient conditions under which randomizing the short side eliminates first-order bias. The first sufficient condition is that almost all short-side participants are matched; this condition holds for the listing side when the market is supply-constrained as they do not hold preferences. The second condition applies when customers are scarce and they don’t concentrate their preferred choices on the same small set of listings. We then give insight into when long-side randomization retains first-order bias.

Throughout the paper, let superscripts SS and LL on match counts correspond to short-side and long-side randomization, respectively. As introduced in Section 2.3, Kn​(𝟎)K_{n}(\mathbf{0}) and Kn​(𝟏)K_{n}(\mathbf{1}) denote match counts under global control and global treatment.

3.1 Bias under near saturation

We first consider markets in which almost every participant on the short side matches. Let KnSK_{n}^{S} be the number of matches in the experiment that randomizes the short side, and recall that Kn​(𝟎)K_{n}(\mathbf{0}) and Kn​(𝟏)K_{n}(\mathbf{1}) are the match counts under global control and global treatment. Since at most mnm_{n} matches can occur, the quantities mn−KnSm_{n}-K_{n}^{S}, mn−Kn​(𝟎)m_{n}-K_{n}(\mathbf{0}), and mn−Kn​(𝟏)m_{n}-K_{n}(\mathbf{1}) count the unmatched participants on the short side in the three regimes.

Proposition 3.1 (Short-side bias under near saturation).

Suppose that, along a sequence of markets with mn→∞m_{n}\to\infty, the expected fraction of short-side participants who are matched converges to one under short-side randomization, global treatment, and global control. That is,

𝔼⁡[KnS]mn⟶1,𝔼​[Kn​(𝐰)]mn⟶1,𝐰∈{𝟎,𝟏}.\frac{\mathbb{E}[K_{n}^{S}]}{m_{n}}\longrightarrow 1,\qquad\frac{\mathbb{E}[K_{n}(\mathbf{w})]}{m_{n}}\longrightarrow 1,\quad\mathbf{w}\in\{\mathbf{0},\mathbf{1}\}. (11)

Then the difference-in-means estimator under short-side randomization satisfies

BS,n=o⁡(sn).B_{S,n}=o(s_{n}).

The intuition is straightforward. If nearly all short-side participants match, their average booking outcomes are close to one in both experiment groups, while total matches are close to mnm_{n} under either global treatment or control market. Consequently, neither the expected value of the difference-in-means estimator nor the global treatment effect can be large relative to sns_{n}. The proof of Proposition 3.1 is in Appendix A. The argument behind the result does not require a particular customer choice model; it uses only the capacity constraints and binary booking outcomes.

Application when listings are scarce.

Near saturation is natural in the FCFS model when listings are the short side and customers are abundant. Listings do not have preferences or reject bookings, so if every customer finds every listing acceptable, all listings are booked after the first mnm_{n} customers arrive.

More generally, it is enough that each listing attracts sufficiently many customers who would choose it if all listings were available. For an experiment design r∈{0,1,S}r\in\{0,1,S\}, let JirJ_{i}^{r} be customer ii’s preferred acceptable listing when all listings are available, with Jir=∅J_{i}^{r}=\varnothing if no listing is acceptable. Let ℰr\mathcal{E}_{r} contain the listing primitives and, in the experiment market, the listing treatment assignments. Conditional on ℰr\mathcal{E}_{r}, the choices JirJ_{i}^{r} are independent across customers.

Proposition 3.2 (A sufficient condition for saturation under FCFS).

Suppose listings are scarce, so NP=mnN_{P}=m_{n} and NC=ℓnN_{C}=\ell_{n}. If there exists c>0c>0 such that for every listing jj and each experiment design r∈{0,1,S}r\in\{0,1,S\},

∑i∈𝒞nPr⁡(Jir=j∣ℰr)≥c​ℓnmnalmost surely,\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}_{n}}\Pr(J_{i}^{r}=j\mid\mathcal{E}_{r})\geq c\frac{\ell_{n}}{m_{n}}\qquad\text{almost surely}, (12)

then

max⁡{𝔼⁡[mn−KnS],𝔼⁡[mn−Kn​(𝐰)]}≤mn​exp⁡(−c​ℓnmn)(𝐰∈{𝟎,𝟏}).\max\left\{\mathbb{E}[m_{n}-K_{n}^{S}],\,\mathbb{E}[m_{n}-K_{n}(\mathbf{w})]\right\}\leq m_{n}\exp\!\left(-c\frac{\ell_{n}}{m_{n}}\right)\qquad(\mathbf{w}\in\{\mathbf{0},\mathbf{1}\}).

In particular, BS,n=o⁡(sn)B_{S,n}=o(s_{n}) as mn/ℓn→0m_{n}/\ell_{n}\to 0 and mn→∞m_{n}\to\infty.

Condition (12) ensures that each listing has a growing expected number of customers who would select it as their first choice. It is sufficient, but not necessary: a listing may also be booked by customers who substitute away from their preferred options. The proof uses the fact that if any customer ranks a listing first, that listing must eventually be booked under FCFS.

3.2 Bias under bounded concentration of customer choice

We next consider the case where customers are scarce. A customer may remain unmatched if they retain a nonvanishing outside option even when listings are abundant, so the saturation condition from the previous subsection need not apply. We instead impose a condition limiting how much competition customers face for the same listings.

For each customer ii and treatment w∈{0,1}w\in\{0,1\}, let Ji(w)∈𝒫n∪{∅}J_{i}^{(w)}\in\mathcal{P}_{n}\cup\{\varnothing\} denote the listing that customer ii would choose under treatment ww if all listings were available. We refer to Ji(w)J_{i}^{(w)} as the customer’s choice in an isolated market. Let ℱP,n\mathcal{F}_{P,n} be the information generated by the listing-specific primitives (ζj)j∈𝒫n(\zeta_{j})_{j\in\mathcal{P}_{n}}.

Assumption 3.3 (Bounded concentration of customer choice).

There is a constant D<∞D<\infty, independent of market size, such that, almost surely,

Pr⁡(Ji(w)=j∣ℱP,n)≤Dℓn,i∈𝒞n,j∈𝒫n,w∈{0,1}.\Pr(J_{i}^{(w)}=j\mid\mathcal{F}_{P,n})\leq\frac{D}{\ell_{n}},\qquad i\in\mathcal{C}_{n},\quad j\in\mathcal{P}_{n},\quad w\in\{0,1\}. (13)

This assumption rules out listings that attract a disproportionately large fraction of scarce customers. It allows heterogeneous preferences and does not require the probabilities to be identical across listings.

Proposition 3.4 (Bias under bounded concentration of customer choices).

Suppose customers are scarce and Assumption 3.3 holds. Then

|BS,n|≤C​mn2n​ℓn+C​sn​e−c​mn|B_{S,n}|\leq C\frac{m_{n}^{2}}{n\ell_{n}}+Cs_{n}e^{-cm_{n}} (14)

for constants C,c>0C,c>0 independent of market size. Consequently,

BS,n=o⁡(sn).B_{S,n}=o(s_{n}).

To understand the result, first consider what each customer would choose if no other customer were present. Under Assumption 3.3, the expected number of pairs of customers that would make the same choice is O⁡(mn2/ℓn)O(m_{n}^{2}/\ell_{n}). These repeated choices bound the number of matches lost because of competition. Since outcomes are normalized by the total market size nn, the resulting bias is of order mn2/(n​ℓn)=O⁡(sn2)m_{n}^{2}/(n\ell_{n})=O(s_{n}^{2}). This gives us the first term in the upper bound. The second term arises from our convention of setting the estimator to zero when one experiment group is empty; this term is exponentially small in mnm_{n}. Thus the bias is always o⁡(sn)o(s_{n}), and when the long-side population grows polynomially with the short-side population, the exponentially small term is negligible and the bias is O⁡(sn2)O(s_{n}^{2}).

3.3 Comparison with long-side randomization

Unlike short-side randomization, long-side randomization can retain first-order bias even in highly imbalanced markets. To see why, let KnLK_{n}^{L} denote the total number of matches under long-side randomization, and let Kn,1LK_{n,1}^{L} denote the number of these matches involving treated participants. The bias satisfies

BL,nsn=1π⁡(1−π)(𝔼⁡[Kn,1L]mn−π𝔼⁡[KnL]mn)−τnsn+O(ℓn−1/2).\frac{B_{L,n}}{s_{n}}=\frac{1}{\pi(1-\pi)}\left(\frac{\mathbb{E}[K_{n,1}^{L}]}{m_{n}}-\pi\frac{\mathbb{E}[K_{n}^{L}]}{m_{n}}\right)-\frac{\tau_{n}}{s_{n}}+O(\ell_{n}^{-1/2}). (15)

The first term captures the extent to which treatment changes the allocation of matches between treated and control participants, while the second captures its effect on the total number of matches. Even when the market is highly imbalanced, these effects need not coincide.

When listings are abundant, making treated listings more attractive can shift bookings away from control listings. When customers are abundant, treated customers may book listings that would otherwise have been available to control customers. In both cases, treatment can change how matches are distributed between experimental groups, even when its effect on the total number of matches under global treatment versus global control is small. This discrepancy can generate first-order interference bias.

We next show that this bias persists in the consideration-set logit model of Johari et al. [19] under natural conditions on the treatment effects.

3.4 An example with logit choice

We conclude this section by showing how the preceding bias results apply within a familiar choice model. We consider the consideration-set logit model of Johari et al. [19], allowing customer preferences, listing attractiveness, and treatment effects to vary across customer–listing pairs.

Suppose customer ii independently considers each available listing jj with probability pi​jwi​jp_{ij}^{w_{ij}}, where wi​j∈{0,1}w_{ij}\in\{0,1\} denotes the treatment exposure of the pair. Conditional on the set ℋi\mathcal{H}_{i} of considered available listings, customer ii books listing j∈ℋij\in\mathcal{H}_{i} with probability

vi​jwi​jηi​NP+∑k∈ℋivi​kwi​k,\frac{v_{ij}^{w_{ij}}}{\eta_{i}N_{P}+\sum_{k\in\mathcal{H}_{i}}v_{ik}^{w_{ik}}}, (16)

where vi​jw>0v_{ij}^{w}>0 is the utility weight of listing jj for customer ii under exposure ww, and ηi​NP>0\eta_{i}N_{P}>0 is the outside-option weight. The remaining probability is assigned to not booking.

We impose the following bounds on the model parameters. There exist positive constants p¯,v¯,v¯,η¯,η¯\underline{p},\underline{v},\overline{v},\underline{\eta},\overline{\eta}, independent of market size, such that for every customer ii, listing jj, and treatment ww,

p¯≤pi​jw≤1,v¯≤vi​jw≤v¯,η¯≤ηi≤η¯.\underline{p}\leq p_{ij}^{w}\leq 1,\qquad\underline{v}\leq v_{ij}^{w}\leq\overline{v},\qquad\underline{\eta}\leq\eta_{i}\leq\overline{\eta}. (17)

These conditions are similar to those in Johari et al. [19], who assume strictly positive consideration probabilities and utility weights, as well as an outside-option weight that scales linearly with the number of listings. In their finite-type model, positivity implies uniform bounds on consideration probabilities and utility weights. We impose these bounds directly to accommodate more general heterogeneity across customers and listings as the market grows.

To establish positive first-order bias under long-side randomization, we additionally consider treatments that increase the expected attractiveness of every customer–listing pair. In particular, if we write ci​jw=pi​jw​vi​jwc_{ij}^{w}=p_{ij}^{w}v_{ij}^{w}, suppose there exists γ>0\gamma>0 independent of market size such that

ci​j1−ci​j0≥γfor all ​i,j.c_{ij}^{1}-c_{ij}^{0}\geq\gamma\qquad\text{for all }i,j. (18)

This condition is similar to the sign-consistency assumption of Johari et al. [20]; it allows heterogeneous treatment effects across customer–listing pairs but requires them to be uniformly positive.

Proposition 3.5 (Bias under logit choice).

Suppose customer choice follows (16), the parameter bounds in (17) hold, and the treatment probability is bounded away from zero and one. Along any sequence with mn→∞m_{n}\to\infty and mn/ℓn→0m_{n}/\ell_{n}\to 0, the following hold.

  1. 1.

    When either side of the market is scarce, short-side randomization eliminates first-order bias:

    BS,n=o⁡(sn).B_{S,n}=o(s_{n}). (19)

    Moreover, when customers are scarce,

    |BS,n|=O⁡(sn2+sn​e−c​mn)|B_{S,n}|=O(s_{n}^{2}+s_{n}e^{-cm_{n}}) (20)

    for some constant c>0c>0.

  2. 2.

    If the sign-consistency condition (18) also holds, then when either side is scarce, long-side randomization retains positive first-order bias:

    lim infn→∞BL,nsn>0,BL,n=Θ⁡(sn).\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{B_{L,n}}{s_{n}}>0,\qquad B_{L,n}=\Theta(s_{n}). (21)

The two conclusions follow from different properties of the choice model. When customers are scarce, the parameter bounds ensure that customers are not too likely to choose the same listings, so the quadratic bias result for short-side randomization applies. When listings are scarce, the bounds ensure that nearly all listings are eventually booked, eliminating first-order short-side bias.

The additional sign-consistency condition ensures that long-side randomization retains first-order bias in both cases. When customers are scarce, treated listings attract bookings that would otherwise go to control listings. When listings are scarce, treated customers are more likely to book the remaining inventory.

4 Variance

Having established the bias results, we now show that in a capacity-constrained marketplace, randomizing on the long side need not reduce variance. Regardless of which side is randomized, the number of matches is limited by the size mnm_{n} of the short side, so participants on the longer side are less likely to match. To illustrate this, suppose booking outcomes on the randomized side dd were independent, with each participant booking with probability pd≍mn/Ndp_{d}\asymp m_{n}/N_{d}. The variance of the rescaled difference-in-means estimator would then be of order

(Ndn)2​pd​(1−pd)Nd=Ndn2​pd​(1−pd).\left(\frac{N_{d}}{n}\right)^{2}\frac{p_{d}(1-p_{d})}{N_{d}}=\frac{N_{d}}{n^{2}}p_{d}(1-p_{d}).

When the long side is randomized, Nd=ℓnN_{d}=\ell_{n} and pd≍mn/ℓn→0p_{d}\asymp m_{n}/\ell_{n}\to 0, so the variance is of order Θ⁡(sn/n)\Theta(s_{n}/n). When the short side is randomized, Nd=mnN_{d}=m_{n}, so the variance is at most O⁡(sn/n)O(s_{n}/n). Thus, despite having a larger sample, long-side randomization need not yield a better variance rate. We next establish when this conclusion holds under FCFS booking, where outcomes are dependent.

4.1 An upper bound for both designs

Our first result holds under the general FCFS model introduced in Section 2, without imposing any additional assumptions on customer preferences.

Proposition 4.1 (Variance upper bound).

Under the assumptions of Section 2, for either d∈{C,P}d\in\{C,P\},

Var⁡(Δ^d,n)=O⁡(mnn2)=O⁡(snn).\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\Delta}_{d,n})=O\left(\frac{m_{n}}{n^{2}}\right)=O\left(\frac{s_{n}}{n}\right). (22)

To understand the result, consider changing the preferences of a single customer or the characteristics of a single listing, while holding everything else fixed. Although this may change which participants are matched to one another, it can change whether at most two customers and two listings are matched. Moreover, if the affected participant remains unmatched both before and after the change, no booking outcomes change. The proof uses these properties, together with the fact that there are at most mnm_{n} matches, to establish the variance bound. It also accounts for the random treatment group sizes in the difference-in-means estimator.

4.2 A lower bound for long-side randomization

The upper bound alone does not rule out a variance advantage for long-side randomization. We next give sufficient conditions under which its variance is at least of order sn/ns_{n}/n. The conditions depend on which side is scarce.

Customers are scarce.

Suppose NC=mnN_{C}=m_{n} and NP=ℓnN_{P}=\ell_{n}, so the long-side experiment randomizes listings. Let ℰn\mathcal{E}_{n} contain the listing primitives and listing treatment assignments, but not the random customer primitives. For an available set A⊆𝒫nA\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{n}, let Ji​(A)J_{i}(A) be the listing that customer ii would choose from AA, with Ji​(A)=∅J_{i}(A)=\varnothing if the customer would not book.

Assumption 4.2 (Bounded choice probabilities and sufficient demand for both experiment groups).

There are constants D<∞D<\infty, α>0\alpha>0, and η>0\eta>0 such that:

  1. 1.

    For every customer ii, every available set AA with |𝒫n∖A|≤mn|\mathcal{P}_{n}\setminus A|\leq m_{n}, and every j∈Aj\in A,

    Pr⁡(Ji​(A)=j∣ℰn)≤Dℓnalmost surely.\Pr(J_{i}(A)=j\mid\mathcal{E}_{n})\leq\frac{D}{\ell_{n}}\quad\text{almost surely}. (23)
  2. 2.

    With probability tending to one, at least α​mn\alpha m_{n} customers satisfy both

    Pr⁡(Ji​(𝒫n)∈𝒫n,1∣ℰn)\displaystyle\Pr\bigl(J_{i}(\mathcal{P}_{n})\in\mathcal{P}_{n,1}\mid\mathcal{E}_{n}\bigr) ≥η,\displaystyle\geq\eta, (24)
    Pr⁡(Ji​(𝒫n)∈𝒫n,0∣ℰn)\displaystyle\Pr\bigl(J_{i}(\mathcal{P}_{n})\in\mathcal{P}_{n,0}\mid\mathcal{E}_{n}\bigr) ≥η,\displaystyle\geq\eta,

    where 𝒫n,w\mathcal{P}_{n,w} is the set of listings assigned to treatment ww.

The first condition requires that when customers are scarce, they are unlikely to choose the same listings, even after earlier bookings have removed some listings. The second condition ensures that both experiment groups attract sufficient potential demand: a nonvanishing fraction of customers have a meaningful probability of choosing a listing from either group. Together, these conditions ensure that competition does not substantially reduce the variation arising from customers’ choices between the two experiment groups.

Listings are scarce.

Now suppose NP=mnN_{P}=m_{n} and NC=ℓnN_{C}=\ell_{n}, so the long-side experiment randomizes customers. Conditional on the listing primitives, write

Qiw​(j∣A):=Pr⁡(customer ​i​ books ​j∣A​ available,WiC=w, listing primitives)Q_{i}^{w}(j\mid A):=\Pr\bigl(\text{customer }i\text{ books }j\mid A\text{ available},\ W_{i}^{C}=w,\text{ listing primitives}\bigr)

for j∈Aj\in A, and define Qiw​(∅∣A)Q_{i}^{w}(\varnothing\mid A) analogously. These probabilities may depend on the customer, the particular listing, and the full available set.

Assumption 4.3 (Treatment has bounded impact on booking).

There are constants 1≤M<∞1\leq M<\infty and κ>0\kappa>0 independent of market size such that, conditional on the listing primitives, for every customer ii, every reachable available set AA, and every j∈Aj\in A,

M−1​Qi0​(j∣A)≤Qi1​(j∣A)≤M​Qi0​(j∣A)almost surely,M^{-1}Q_{i}^{0}(j\mid A)\leq Q_{i}^{1}(j\mid A)\leq MQ_{i}^{0}(j\mid A)\quad\text{almost surely}, (25)

and the expected number of matches in the customer-randomized experiment satisfies

𝔼⁡[KnL]≥κ​mn.\mathbb{E}[K_{n}^{L}]\geq\kappa m_{n}. (26)

The first condition requires a booking of a particular listing to remain possible under both customer treatment assignments with comparable probabilities. The condition allows customers and listings to differ in their characteristics and preferences, as well as in how treatment affects their choices. The second condition requires that the expected number of matched listings is at least a constant fraction of all listings.

Under these conditions, we can show that randomizing on the long side retains substantial variance. The intuition is that even after observing which customers successfully book, there is uncertainty about their treatment assignments which generates meaningful variance in the estimator.

Theorem 4.4 (Variance under long-side randomization).

Suppose mn,ℓn→∞m_{n},\ell_{n}\to\infty and mn/ℓn→0m_{n}/\ell_{n}\to 0. If customers are scarce, impose Assumption 4.2. If listings are scarce, impose Assumption 4.3. Then

Var⁡(Δ^L,n)=Θ⁡(mnn2)=Θ⁡(snn).\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\Delta}_{L,n})=\Theta\left(\frac{m_{n}}{n^{2}}\right)=\Theta\left(\frac{s_{n}}{n}\right). (27)

Consequently,

Var⁡(Δ^S,n)=O⁡(Var⁡(Δ^L,n)).\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\Delta}_{S,n})=O\bigl(\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\Delta}_{L,n})\bigr).

The intuition behind these results is that although the long side contains more participants, the number of matches is limited by the size of the short side. Consequently, the larger sample does not necessarily translate into a lower variance rate. The key is to show that there remains sufficient variation in how matches are distributed between treatment and control. When customers are scarce, customers are not overly likely to choose the same listings, so competition does not substantially reduce this variation. When listings are scarce, customers have comparable probabilities of booking a given listing under treatment and control, so observing which customers successfully book does not fully reveal their treatment assignments.

4.3 Variance comparison under logit choice

We now apply our variance results to the consideration-set logit model introduced in Section 3.4. The same logit parameter bounds in (17) that guarantee vanishing first-order bias under short-side randomization also ensure that long-side randomization cannot achieve a smaller asymptotic variance.

Corollary 4.5 (Variance comparison under logit choice).

Suppose customer choice follows (16), the parameter bounds in (17) hold, and the treatment probabilities are bounded away from zero and one. Then, when either customers or listings are scarce,

Var⁡(Δ^S,n)=O⁡(snn),Var⁡(Δ^L,n)=Θ⁡(snn).\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\Delta}_{S,n})=O\left(\frac{s_{n}}{n}\right),\qquad\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\Delta}_{L,n})=\Theta\left(\frac{s_{n}}{n}\right).

When customers are scarce, the parameter bounds ensure that customers are not overly likely to compete for the same listings, while both treated and control listings retain a positive probability of being chosen. When listings are scarce, the bounds ensure that treatment and control customers have comparable probabilities of booking any available listing. Consequently, the larger nominal sample under long-side randomization does not yield a smaller asymptotic variance rate.

Together with Proposition 3.5, this corollary shows that short-side randomization eliminates first-order bias without having a worse variance rate.

5 Conclusion

Our results suggest that platforms should generally favor short-side randomization when designing experiments in two-sided marketplaces. Under relatively mild conditions satisfied by familiar logit models of customer choice, short-side randomization reduces interference bias while achieving an asymptotic variance rate no worse than long-side randomization. This challenges the conventional intuition that randomizing on the larger side necessarily yields lower variance: although the long side provides a larger nominal sample, the number of matches is constrained by the short-side population, limiting the benefit of randomizing more participants. An important direction for future work is to develop practical methods for selecting the randomized side based on observable market characteristics.

Appendix A Proofs for Section 3

This appendix proves the bias results in Section 3. The main ingredient is a simple property of sequential booking: a listing that is someone’s first acceptable choice when all listings are available must be booked in the full market. This observation allows us to bound the effect of competition without restricting how customers rank their remaining options.

A.1 First choices and match count losses

Fix a realization of the market and a vector of treatments 𝐰\mathbf{w}. For each customer ii, let Ji∈𝒫n∪{∅}J_{i}\in\mathcal{P}_{n}\cup\{\varnothing\} be the listing customer ii would choose if all listings were available, with Ji=∅J_{i}=\varnothing if none is acceptable. Write Ai=𝟏{Ji≠∅}A_{i}=\mathbf{1}\{J_{i}\neq\varnothing\} and let YiY_{i} denote the customer’s actual booking indicator under FCFS.

Lemma A.1 (Bounding the number of lost matches).

Let U={Ji:Ji≠∅}U=\{J_{i}:J_{i}\neq\varnothing\} be the set of distinct nonempty first-choice listings, and let KK be the number of mstches. Then UU is contained in the set of booked listings and

0\displaystyle 0 ≤∑i∈𝒞n(Ai−Yi)=∑i∈𝒞nAi−K\displaystyle\leq\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}_{n}}(A_{i}-Y_{i})=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}_{n}}A_{i}-K (28)
≤∑i∈𝒞nAi−|U|\displaystyle\leq\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}_{n}}A_{i}-|U|
≤∑i,k∈𝒞ni<k𝟏{Ji=Jk≠∅}.\displaystyle\leq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,k\in\mathcal{C}_{n}\\ i<k\end{subarray}}\mathbf{1}\{J_{i}=J_{k}\neq\varnothing\}.
Proof.

If customer ii has no acceptable listing when all listings are available, the customer cannot match in the full market. Therefore Yi≤AiY_{i}\leq A_{i} for every ii, proving the first inequality.

Consider any listing j∈Uj\in U. If jj has already been booked when a customer with first choice jj arrives, then jj is matched in the final allocation. Otherwise that customer finds jj available and selects it, because jj is their highest-ranked acceptable listing. In either case, jj is eventually booked. Hence K≥|U|K\geq|U|.

For each listing jj, let dj=∑i𝟏{Ji=j}d_{j}=\sum_{i}\mathbf{1}\{J_{i}=j\}. We have

∑iAi−|U|=∑j∈𝒫ndj−∑j∈𝒫n𝟏dj≥1=∑j∈𝒫n(dj−1)+.\sum_{i}A_{i}-|U|=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{P}_{n}}d_{j}-\sum_{j\in\mathcal{P}_{n}}\mathbf{1}_{d_{j}\geq 1}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{P}_{n}}(d_{j}-1)_{+}.

For every nonnegative integer dd, (d−1)+≤(d2)(d-1)_{+}\leq\binom{d}{2}. Thus,

∑j∈𝒫n(dj−1)+≤∑j∈𝒫n(dj2).\sum_{j\in\mathcal{P}_{n}}(d_{j}-1)_{+}\leq\sum_{j\in\mathcal{P}_{n}}\binom{d_{j}}{2}.

The sum over listings gives the final inequality in (28), since ∑j(dj2)\sum_{j}\binom{d_{j}}{2} counts pairs of customers with the same nonempty first choice. ∎

The lemma above bounds the number of matches lost relative to a market where customers could choose whatever they want regardless of capacity constraints.

A.3 Bounded concentration of customer choices

Proof of Proposition 3.4.

Throughout this proof customers are the short side, so NC=mnN_{C}=m_{n} and NP=ℓnN_{P}=\ell_{n}. For w∈{0,1}w\in\{0,1\}, define Ai(w)=𝟏{Ji(w)≠∅}A_{i}^{(w)}=\mathbf{1}\{J_{i}^{(w)}\neq\varnothing\}. Let

τ~n=1n​∑i∈𝒞n(𝔼⁡[Ai(1)]−𝔼⁡[Ai(0)])\widetilde{\tau}_{n}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}_{n}}\left(\mathbb{E}[A_{i}^{(1)}]-\mathbb{E}[A_{i}^{(0)}]\right) (32)

be the global treatment effect that would arise if every customer could make their choice in isolation without competing with other customers. Note that in the absence of competition, the resulting difference-in-means estimator would be unbiased.

Step 1: Bounding the effect of competition on bookings.

Conditional on ℱP,n\mathcal{F}_{P,n}, the random variables Ji(w)J_{i}^{(w)} are independent across customers. For distinct i,ki,k, Assumption 3.3 gives

Pr⁡(Ji(w)=Jk(w)≠∅∣ℱP,n)\displaystyle\Pr(J_{i}^{(w)}=J_{k}^{(w)}\neq\varnothing\mid\mathcal{F}_{P,n}) =∑j∈𝒫nPr⁡(Ji(w)=j∣ℱP,n)​Pr⁡(Jk(w)=j∣ℱP,n)\displaystyle=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{P}_{n}}\Pr(J_{i}^{(w)}=j\mid\mathcal{F}_{P,n})\Pr(J_{k}^{(w)}=j\mid\mathcal{F}_{P,n}) (33)
≤Dℓn.\displaystyle\leq\frac{D}{\ell_{n}}.

Lemma A.1 therefore implies

0≤∑i𝔼⁡[Ai(w)]−𝔼⁡[Kn​(𝐰)]≤Dℓn​(mn2),w∈{0,1}.0\leq\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}[A_{i}^{(w)}]-\mathbb{E}[K_{n}(\mathbf{w})]\leq\frac{D}{\ell_{n}}\binom{m_{n}}{2},\qquad w\in\{0,1\}.

Taking the difference between the true GATE and the isolated-market GATE and applying the triangle inequality yields

|τn−τ~n|≤D​mn​(mn−1)n​ℓn.|\tau_{n}-\widetilde{\tau}_{n}|\leq\frac{D\,m_{n}(m_{n}-1)}{n\ell_{n}}. (34)

Step 2: Bounding the effect of competition on the estimator.

For customer randomization, let AiS=Ai(WiC)A_{i}^{S}=A_{i}^{(W_{i}^{C})} and define

Δ~S,n=mnn(∑i:WiC=1Ai(1)NS,1−∑i:WiC=0Ai(0)NS,0),\widetilde{\Delta}_{S,n}=\frac{m_{n}}{n}\left(\frac{\sum_{i:W_{i}^{C}=1}A_{i}^{(1)}}{N_{S,1}}-\frac{\sum_{i:W_{i}^{C}=0}A_{i}^{(0)}}{N_{S,0}}\right), (35)

with the same convention that if an experiment group is empty then the corresponding term is zero.

Let ℬi−1\mathcal{B}_{i-1} be the set of listings booked before customer ii arrives in the experiment. Conditional on ℱP,n\mathcal{F}_{P,n} and the full customer assignment vector, ℬi−1\mathcal{B}_{i-1} depends only on earlier customers’ random inputs and is independent of Ji(WiC)J_{i}^{(W_{i}^{C})}. ≤D⁡(i−1)ℓn.\displaystyle\leq\frac{D(i-1)}{\ell_{n}}.

When both experiment groups are nonempty, the difference between Δ~S,n\widetilde{\Delta}_{S,n} and Δ^S,n\widehat{\Delta}_{S,n} is bounded by the average number of bookings lost to competition in each group. Applying (36) for any realized treatment assignment vector with nonempty groups implies

≤mnn(1NS,1∑i:WiC=1D⁡(i−1)ℓn+1NS,0∑i:WiC=0D⁡(i−1)ℓn)\displaystyle\leq\frac{m_{n}}{n}\left(\frac{1}{N_{S,1}}\sum_{i:W_{i}^{C}=1}\frac{D(i-1)}{\ell_{n}}+\frac{1}{N_{S,0}}\sum_{i:W_{i}^{C}=0}\frac{D(i-1)}{\ell_{n}}\right)

Appendix B Proofs for the Variance Results

For d∈{C,P}d\in\{C,P\}, let 𝒟d\mathcal{D}_{d} denote the randomized side, let Nd=|𝒟d|N_{d}=|\mathcal{D}_{d}|, and let πd\pi_{d} be its treatment probability. Recall the experiment group match counts Kd,wK_{d,w} from (7). Write

Hd,n:=n​Δ^d,nHT=Kd,1πd−Kd,01−πdH_{d,n}:=n\widehat{\Delta}^{\mathrm{HT}}_{d,n}=\frac{K_{d,1}}{\pi_{d}}-\frac{K_{d,0}}{1-\pi_{d}} (42)

for the scaled Horvitz–Thompson (HT) estimator. We first establish two finite-market lemmas that transfer variance bounds for Hd,nH_{d,n} to the actual difference-in-means estimator.

Lemma B.1 (Bounded sensitivity of match statuses).

Consider two FCFS markets with the same arrival order and all primitives identical except the primitives of one customer or one listing. The final matched/unmatched indicators differ for at most two customers and at most two listings. If the changed participant is unmatched in both markets, the booking choices of every participant are identical.

Proof.

We compare markets through a common market in which the changed participant is removed. All preferences of participants other than the changed participant over their remaining options are the same in these comparisons, as required by condition (1).

First suppose that listing jj is changed. Compare either version of the original market with a market in which jj is unavailable from the outset. At every arrival, the available set in the market with jj is either the same as, or consists of one additional listing relative to, the available set without jj. To see this, initially the difference is {j}\{j\}. If both customers choose the same listing in the two markets, the difference is unchanged. If their choices differ, the customer in the market with jj must choose its one extra listing since the rankings over all listings common to both markets agree. The customer in the market without jj either chooses a listing common to both markets (which then becomes the new extra listing in the larger market) or chooses no listing (in which case the two available sets become equal and stay equal). Hence a customer can book in the market with jj but not in the market without jj at most once; the reverse cannot occur.

Both versions of the original market can be compared with the same reference market in which jj is unavailable. Since each version differs from the reference market in the booking status of at most one customer, the two versions differ in the booking statuses of at most two customers. Similarly, the final set of available listings in each version differs from that of the reference market by at most one listing. Thus, the two versions differ in the booking statuses of at most two listings.

Now suppose that customer ii is changed. Compare either version with the market that skips customer ii in the arrival order. The histories or arrivals and bookings coincide before ii arrives. Immediately after that arrival, the market containing ii has either the same available set or one fewer available listing. The same induction as when we excluded one listing, with the inclusion reversed, shows that among customers other than ii, at most one additional customer can fail to book when ii is present. The difference in final listing booking indicators is at most one for each comparison with the market without ii. If ii books in both versions, the two possibly displaced customers are the only customers whose booking statuses can differ; if ii books in just one version, at most ii and one displaced customer can differ. Thus there are at most two different customer match statuses and at most two different listing match statuses.

Finally, if a changed customer never books in either version of the market, its arrival does not change the available set, and all subsequent choices agree. Similarly, suppose listing jj is not booked in either version of the market. If the two booking histories differed between the two markets, consider the first customer whose booking decision differs. At that arrival, the same listings are available in both markets, and customer preferences over all listings other than jj agree. Therefore, any difference in the customer’s booking decision must involve booking jj in at least one market, contradicting the assumption. Hence the two booking histories are identical. ∎

Lemma B.2 (Random experiment group sizes).

Suppose ε≤πd≤1−ε\varepsilon\leq\pi_{d}\leq 1-\varepsilon and Nd→∞N_{d}\to\infty. With the convention in (8) for handling empty expreiment groups, there is a constant Cε<∞C_{\varepsilon}<\infty such that

𝔼⁡[(n​Δ^d,n−Hd,n)2]≤Cε​mn2Nd.\mathbb{E}\left[\bigl(n\widehat{\Delta}_{d,n}-H_{d,n}\bigr)^{2}\right]\leq C_{\varepsilon}\frac{m_{n}^{2}}{N_{d}}. (43)

In particular, for long-side randomization with mn/ℓn→0m_{n}/\ell_{n}\to 0, the right-hand side is o⁡(mn)o(m_{n}).

Proof.

Suppress d,nd,n. Write N=NdN=N_{d}, m=mnm=m_{n}, π=πd\pi=\pi_{d}, and T=Nd,1∼Binomial⁡(N,π)T=N_{d,1}\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(N,\pi). On the event ℬ={|T−πN|≤εN/2}\mathcal{B}=\{|T-\pi N|\leq\varepsilon N/2\}, both experiment groups are nonempty, and

|n​Δ^−H|\displaystyle|n\widehat{\Delta}-H| ≤Kd,1​|NT−1π|+Kd,0​|NN−T−11−π|\displaystyle\leq K_{d,1}\left|\frac{N}{T}-\frac{1}{\pi}\right|+K_{d,0}\left|\frac{N}{N-T}-\frac{1}{1-\pi}\right|
≤Cε​(Kd,1+Kd,0)​|T−π​N|N\displaystyle\leq C_{\varepsilon}(K_{d,1}+K_{d,0})\frac{|T-\pi N|}{N}
≤Cε​m​|T−π​N|N.\displaystyle\leq C_{\varepsilon}m\frac{|T-\pi N|}{N}.

The first two inequalities are deterministic and do not require independence between the size of the experiment groups and the match counts. Since 𝔼⁡[(T−π​N)2]=N​π​(1−π)\mathbb{E}[(T-\pi N)^{2}]=N\pi(1-\pi),

𝔼⁡[(n​Δ^−H)2​𝟏ℬ]≤Cε​m2/N.\mathbb{E}\bigl[(n\widehat{\Delta}-H)^{2}\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{B}}\bigr]\leq C_{\varepsilon}m^{2}/N.

On ℬc\mathcal{B}^{c}, the rescaled difference in means is bounded by NN in absolute value, including when an experiment group is empty, and |H|≤m/ε|H|\leq m/\varepsilon. Hoeffding’s inequality gives Pr⁡(ℬc)≤2​e−cε​N\Pr(\mathcal{B}^{c})\leq 2e^{-c_{\varepsilon}N}. As 1≤m≤N1\leq m\leq N, the resulting contribution Cε​N2​e−cε​NC_{\varepsilon}N^{2}e^{-c_{\varepsilon}N} is at most Cε​m2/NC_{\varepsilon}m^{2}/N after increasing the constant if needed. This proves the claim. When N=ℓnN=\ell_{n}, we have mn2/ℓn=o⁡(mn)m_{n}^{2}/\ell_{n}=o(m_{n}). ∎

Proof of Proposition 4.1.

For each participant vv, collect its random primitives and, if it is on the randomized side, its treatment assignment into one block XvX_{v}. These nn blocks are independent under the setup of Section 2. Let Xv′X_{v}^{\prime} be an independent copy of XvX_{v}, and let Hd,n(v)H_{d,n}^{(v)} denote the resulting scaled HT estimator (42) after replacing XvX_{v} with Xv′X_{v}^{\prime}.

By Lemma B.1, replacing one block changes the booking statuses of at most two participants on the randomized side. If vv is itself on the randomized side, its treatment assignment may also change, affecting only its own coefficient in Hd,nH_{d,n} as it gets included in a different experiment group. Since the coefficients in the scaled HT estimator are bounded in absolute value by 1/ε1/\varepsilon, there exists a constant CεC_{\varepsilon} such that

|Hd,n−Hd,n(v)|≤Cε.|H_{d,n}-H_{d,n}^{(v)}|\leq C_{\varepsilon}.

Furthermore, the lemma establishes that if vv is unmatched in both the original and resampled markets, the booking histories are identical. In this case, the scaled HT estimator is unchanged, even if vv’s treatment assignment changes. Combining these two observations and enlarging CεC_{\varepsilon} if necessary gives

(Hd,n−Hd,n(v))2≤Cε​𝟏​{v​ is matched in at least one of the two markets}.(H_{d,n}-H_{d,n}^{(v)})^{2}\leq C_{\varepsilon}\mathbf{1}\{v\text{ is matched in at least one of the two markets}\}.

𝔼⁡[(Hd,n−Hd,n(v))2]≤Cε​{Pr⁡(v​ matched)+Pr⁡(v​ matched after resampling)}.\mathbb{E}[(H_{d,n}-H_{d,n}^{(v)})^{2}]\leq C_{\varepsilon}\bigl\{\Pr(v\text{ matched})+\Pr(v\text{ matched after resampling})\bigr\}.

We now apply the Efron–Stein inequality to obtain

Var⁡(Hd,n)\displaystyle\operatorname{Var}(H_{d,n}) ≤12​∑v𝔼⁡[(Hd,n−Hd,n(v))2]\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{v}\mathbb{E}[(H_{d,n}-H_{d,n}^{(v)})^{2}]
≤Cε​∑v{Pr⁡(v​ matched)+Pr⁡(v​ matched after resampling)}\displaystyle\leq C_{\varepsilon}\sum_{v}\bigl\{\Pr(v\text{ matched})+\Pr(v\text{ matched after resampling})\bigr\}
=4​Cε​𝔼​[Knd]≤4​Cε​mn.\displaystyle=4C_{\varepsilon}\mathbb{E}[K_{n}^{d}]\leq 4C_{\varepsilon}m_{n}.

The equality follows because each booking matches one customer and one listing, so the sum of matching probabilities across all participants equals twice the expected number of bookings. The same holds after resampling, since the resampled market has the same distribution as the original market.

Lemma B.2 now implies

Var⁡(n​Δ^d,n)\displaystyle\operatorname{Var}(n\widehat{\Delta}_{d,n}) ≤2​Var⁡(Hd,n)+2​𝔼​[(n​Δ^d,n−Hd,n)2]\displaystyle\leq 2\operatorname{Var}(H_{d,n})+2\mathbb{E}[(n\widehat{\Delta}_{d,n}-H_{d,n})^{2}]
≤Cε​(mn+mn2Nd)=O⁡(mn),\displaystyle\leq C_{\varepsilon}\left(m_{n}+\frac{m_{n}^{2}}{N_{d}}\right)=O(m_{n}),

since Nd≥mnN_{d}\geq m_{n}. Dividing by n2n^{2} proves the proposition. ∎

Proof of Theorem 4.4: customers scarce.

Suppose NC=mnN_{C}=m_{n} and NP=ℓnN_{P}=\ell_{n}, and write m=mnm=m_{n} and ℓ=ℓn\ell=\ell_{n}. Condition on ℰn\mathcal{E}_{n}, which contains the listing primitives and their treatment labels. Set a1=1/πPa_{1}=1/\pi_{P} and a0=−1/(1−πP)a_{0}=-1/(1-\pi_{P}). For each customer define the contribution of each customer to the HT estimator in the isolated market as

Gi={a1,Ji​(𝒫n)∈𝒫n,1,a0,Ji​(𝒫n)∈𝒫n,0,0,Ji​(𝒫n)=∅.G_{i}=\begin{cases}a_{1},&J_{i}(\mathcal{P}_{n})\in\mathcal{P}_{n,1},\\ a_{0},&J_{i}(\mathcal{P}_{n})\in\mathcal{P}_{n,0},\\ 0,&J_{i}(\mathcal{P}_{n})=\varnothing.\end{cases}

The GiG_{i} are independent conditional on ℰn\mathcal{E}_{n}, because the customer inputs are independent. For a customer satisfying (24), write pi​1=Pr⁡(Gi=a1∣ℰn)p_{i1}=\Pr(G_{i}=a_{1}\mid\mathcal{E}_{n}) and pi​0=Pr⁡(Gi=a0∣ℰn)p_{i0}=\Pr(G_{i}=a_{0}\mid\mathcal{E}_{n}). The variance identity for a finite-valued random variable gives

Var⁡(Gi∣ℰn)≥pi​1​pi​0​(a1−a0)2≥η2​(a1−a0)2.\operatorname{Var}(G_{i}\mid\mathcal{E}_{n})\geq p_{i1}p_{i0}(a_{1}-a_{0})^{2}\geq\eta^{2}(a_{1}-a_{0})^{2}.

Consequently, on the event that at least α​m\alpha m customers satisfy the overlap condition,

Var⁡(∑i=1mGi|ℰn)≥c​m.\operatorname{Var}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}G_{i}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{E}_{n}\right)\geq cm. (44)

The event has probability tending to one.

Write

HL,n=∑i=1mGi+Rn,H_{L,n}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}G_{i}+R_{n},

where RnR_{n} is the correction due to competition for previously booked listings. We establish

Var⁡(Rn∣ℰn)≤C​m2ℓ.\operatorname{Var}(R_{n}\mid\mathcal{E}_{n})\leq C\frac{m^{2}}{\ell}. (45)

To do so, independently resample the full input of customer ii, keeping the other customer inputs and ℰn\mathcal{E}_{n} fixed, and write Rn(i)R_{n}^{(i)} for the resulting correction. The two booking histories agree before customer ii arrives. By (23) and independence from preceding customers, either the original or the resampled isolated first choice of customer ii is already booked with conditional probability at most D​m/ℓDm/\ell.

On the complement of these two events, customer ii books its isolated first choice in both histories, or chooses the outside option in one or both. The available sets immediately afterward differ by at most one listing in each direction. For any later customer, before the first difference in its choices in the two histories, choosing differently requires choosing a listing in the symmetric difference of the available sets. There are at most two such listings, and, conditional on the prior history and ℰn\mathcal{E}_{n}, the probability that this customer chooses one of them is at most 2​D/ℓ2D/\ell by (23). A union bound over at most mm subsequent customers therefore gives

Pr⁡(Rn≠Rn(i)∣ℰn)≤C​mℓ.\Pr(R_{n}\neq R_{n}^{(i)}\mid\mathcal{E}_{n})\leq C\frac{m}{\ell}.

When neither of these events occurs, the change in HL,nH_{L,n} is exactly the change in GiG_{i}, so the correction is unchanged. By Lemma B.1, the change in HL,nH_{L,n} is uniformly bounded; the change in GiG_{i} is also uniformly bounded. Thus |Rn−Rn(i)|≤Cε|R_{n}-R_{n}^{(i)}|\leq C_{\varepsilon}, and conditional Efron–Stein yields

Var⁡(Rn∣ℰn)≤12​∑i=1m𝔼⁡[(Rn−Rn(i))2∣ℰn]≤C​m2ℓ.\operatorname{Var}(R_{n}\mid\mathcal{E}_{n})\leq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{E}[(R_{n}-R_{n}^{(i)})^{2}\mid\mathcal{E}_{n}]\leq C\frac{m^{2}}{\ell}.

This proves (45).

On the event where the overlap condition holds, the reverse triangle inequality for conditional standard deviations now gives

Var⁡(HL,n∣ℰn)≥c​m−C​m2/ℓ.\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(H_{L,n}\mid\mathcal{E}_{n})}\geq\sqrt{cm}-\sqrt{Cm^{2}/\ell}.

Since m/ℓ→0m/\ell\to 0, this is at least c′​mc^{\prime}\sqrt{m} for sufficiently large nn. The overlap event has probability tending to one, so the law of total variance implies Var⁡(HL,n)≥c′′​m\operatorname{Var}(H_{L,n})\geq c^{\prime\prime}m. Finally, Lemma B.2 gives 𝔼⁡[(n​Δ^L,n−HL,n)2]=o⁡(m)\mathbb{E}[(n\widehat{\Delta}_{L,n}-H_{L,n})^{2}]=o(m). The reverse triangle inequality for unconditional standard deviations then proves Var⁡(Δ^L,n)=Ω⁡(m/n2)\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\Delta}_{L,n})=\Omega(m/n^{2}). ∎

Proof of Theorem 4.4: listings scarce.

Suppose NP=mnN_{P}=m_{n} and NC=ℓnN_{C}=\ell_{n}. Write m=mnm=m_{n}, ℓ=ℓn\ell=\ell_{n}, and π=πC\pi=\pi_{C}. Let ℰn\mathcal{E}_{n} contain all listing inputs, and condition on ℰn\mathcal{E}_{n} throughout the next argument. Consider the complete booking trajectory 𝒯=(J1,…,Jℓ)\mathcal{T}=(J_{1},\ldots,J_{\ell}). For any realized trajectory t=(j1,…,jℓ)t=(j_{1},\ldots,j_{\ell}), the available set immediately before customer ii is a deterministic function Ai​(t)A_{i}(t) of the earlier choices. In particular, it does not depend on treatment assignments once the trajectory is specified. Because the customer inputs and treatment assignments are independent across arrivals,

Pr⁡(W=w,𝒯=t∣ℰn)=∏i=1ℓπwi​(1−π)1−wi​Qiwi​(ji∣Ai​(t)).\Pr(W=w,\mathcal{T}=t\mid\mathcal{E}_{n})=\prod_{i=1}^{\ell}\pi^{w_{i}}(1-\pi)^{1-w_{i}}Q_{i}^{w_{i}}(j_{i}\mid A_{i}(t)). (46)

Here Qiw​(∅∣A)Q_{i}^{w}(\varnothing\mid A) denotes the probability of no booking. The factorization applies to any trajectory of positive probability.

Bayes’ rule applied to (46) shows that, conditional on (𝒯,ℰn)(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{E}_{n}), the labels WiW_{i} are independent Bernoulli variables with probabilities

ρi​(𝒯)=π​Qi1​(Ji∣Ai)π​Qi1​(Ji∣Ai)+(1−π)​Qi0​(Ji∣Ai).\rho_{i}(\mathcal{T})=\frac{\pi Q_{i}^{1}(J_{i}\mid A_{i})}{\pi Q_{i}^{1}(J_{i}\mid A_{i})+(1-\pi)Q_{i}^{0}(J_{i}\mid A_{i})}. (47)

For every realized booking, the probability of making that choice averaged over the two treatment assignments is strictly positive. Under (25), either both booking probabilities are positive or neither is, so their ratio lies between M−1M^{-1} and MM on every realized booking. Since ε≤π≤1−ε\varepsilon\leq\pi\leq 1-\varepsilon, there is a constant η>0\eta>0, independent of nn, such that for all customers with Ji≠∅J_{i}\neq\varnothing,

η≤ρi​(𝒯)≤1−η.\eta\leq\rho_{i}(\mathcal{T})\leq 1-\eta. (48)

No such bound is needed for customers who do not book.

Recall that

HL,n=∑i=1ℓ𝟏{Ji≠∅}(Wiπ−1−Wi1−π).H_{L,n}=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\mathbf{1}\{J_{i}\neq\varnothing\}\left(\frac{W_{i}}{\pi}-\frac{1-W_{i}}{1-\pi}\right).

The booked indicators are fixed by 𝒯\mathcal{T}. The conditional independence just proved gives

Var⁡(HL,n∣𝒯,ℰn)\displaystyle\operatorname{Var}(H_{L,n}\mid\mathcal{T},\mathcal{E}_{n}) =1π2​(1−π)2∑i:Ji≠∅ρi(𝒯)(1−ρi(𝒯))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\pi^{2}(1-\pi)^{2}}\sum_{i:J_{i}\neq\varnothing}\rho_{i}(\mathcal{T})(1-\rho_{i}(\mathcal{T}))
≥c​KnL.\displaystyle\geq cK_{n}^{L}. (49)

Var⁡(HL,n)≥𝔼⁡[Var⁡(HL,n∣𝒯,ℰn)]≥c​𝔼​[KnL]≥c​κ​m.\operatorname{Var}(H_{L,n})\geq\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(H_{L,n}\mid\mathcal{T},\mathcal{E}_{n})]\geq c\mathbb{E}[K_{n}^{L}]\geq c\kappa m.

Finally, Lemma B.2 gives 𝔼⁡[(n​Δ^L,n−HL,n)2]≤C​m2/ℓ=o⁡(m)\mathbb{E}[(n\widehat{\Delta}_{L,n}-H_{L,n})^{2}]\leq Cm^{2}/\ell=o(m). The reverse triangle inequality for standard deviations therefore gives Var⁡(Δ^L,n)=Ω⁡(m/n2)\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\Delta}_{L,n})=\Omega(m/n^{2}). Proof of Corollary 4.5.

The example is compatible with the utility rankings in Section 2. For instance, give customer ii independent standard Gumbel shocks Gi​jG_{ij} for the listings and Gi​0G_{i0} for the outside option, and generate each potential consideration indicator Ci​j​(w)C_{ij}(w) from customer-specific random inputs. ui​j​(w)=log⁡vi​jw+Gi​j−log⁡(ηi​NP)−Gi​0;u_{ij}(w)=\log v_{ij}^{w}+G_{ij}-\log(\eta_{i}N_{P})-G_{i0};

The logit probabilities then arise from maximizing these utilities over the considered available listings and the outside option, and each customer has a fixed ranking across available sets. The random inputs are independent across customers and local to the pair utilities, as required in Section 2.

Write

The denominator is always between η¯​NP\underline{\eta}N_{P} and (η¯+v¯)​NP(\overline{\eta}+\overline{v})N_{P}; the numerator is positive when jj is considered, an event of probability at least p¯\underline{p}. Therefore

c−NP≤Pr⁡(Ji​(A)=j∣𝐰, listing inputs)≤c+NP(j∈A).\frac{c_{-}}{N_{P}}\leq\Pr(J_{i}(A)=j\mid\mathbf{w},\text{ listing inputs})\leq\frac{c_{+}}{N_{P}}\qquad(j\in A). (50)

First suppose customers are scarce, so NP=ℓnN_{P}=\ell_{n}. The upper bound in (50) verifies (23) for every available set. By concentration of the independent listing assignments, with probability tending to one both experiment groups contain at least ε​ℓn/2\varepsilon\ell_{n}/2 listings. On that event, (50) implies for every customer ii and both w∈{0,1}w\in\{0,1\},

Now suppose listings are scarce, so NP=mn=mN_{P}=m_{n}=m and NC=ℓn=ℓN_{C}=\ell_{n}=\ell. Under customer randomization, for each available listing jj and treatment state ww,

c−m≤Qiw​(j∣A)≤c+m.\frac{c_{-}}{m}\leq Q_{i}^{w}(j\mid A)\leq\frac{c_{+}}{m}.

Thus (25) holds with M=c+/c−M=c_{+}/c_{-}. (The constants satisfy c+≥c−c_{+}\geq c_{-} because they bound the same nonzero choice probabilities.) Moreover, if rr listings remain just before an arrival, the conditional booking probability is at least c−​r/mc_{-}r/m. If RtR_{t} is the number of listings remaining after tt customer arrivals, independence of the arriving customer’s input from the preceding history gives

𝔼⁡[Rt+1∣Rt=r]≤r⁡(1−c−m).\mathbb{E}[R_{t+1}\mid R_{t}=r]\leq r\left(1-\frac{c_{-}}{m}\right).

𝔼⁡[m−KnL]=𝔼⁡[Rℓ]≤m​(1−c−m)ℓ≤m​exp⁡(−c−​ℓm)=o⁡(m).\mathbb{E}[m-K_{n}^{L}]=\mathbb{E}[R_{\ell}]\leq m\left(1-\frac{c_{-}}{m}\right)^{\ell}\leq m\exp\left(-c_{-}\frac{\ell}{m}\right)=o(m).

Ordinary logit with heterogeneous baseline weights.

For completeness, consider the listing-scarce regime with ordinary logit probabilities

Qiw​(j∣A)=vi​jwvi​0w+∑k∈Avi​kw.Q_{i}^{w}(j\mid A)=\frac{v_{ij}^{w}}{v_{i0}^{w}+\sum_{k\in A}v_{ik}^{w}}.

ab≤Qi1​(j∣A)Qi0​(j∣A)≤ba.\frac{a}{b}\leq\frac{Q_{i}^{1}(j\mid A)}{Q_{i}^{0}(j\mid A)}\leq\frac{b}{a}.
